author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Folding Chairs and Honest Labor
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass two
content:
Greg had agreed to perform at a fundraiser before anyone told him there was no one assigned to put away the chairs.

That was how I found him at Starwake Pier, holding a box of tangled lantern cords in one hand and a folding table under his other arm.

"How's the glamorous life of a musician?" I asked.

"Nobody warned me about furniture."

"Did you read the volunteer sheet?"

"Yep."

"Did you put your own name next to every empty task?"

Greg glanced at the paper pinned to a post. Nearly every line had GREG written beside it.

"That is a wildly unfair accusation," he said. "Some of those say 'Greg U.'"

He was trying to make me laugh, which was ordinarily a successful strategy. I took the table from him instead.

"You're performing tonight. You also have sound checks, and you're supposed to make sure the speakers don't blow the fuse again. You can't do everything."

"I know."

"You don't sound convinced."

Greg set the cords down.

"People need the money. The pier needs new supports. If somebody says they'll do a job and then doesn't, I can at least make sure it happens."

"I know why you do it. That doesn't make the plan workable."

He rubbed his face. The sun caught on the edges of his hair.

"Do you have a better plan?"

"I was hoping we could make one together."

We began with the chairs. There were forty-eight of them, three with loose hinges and one whose left leg did not quite touch the ground. I wrote the number at the top of the volunteer sheet and set the broken ones aside.

Greg inspected the crooked chair.

"Hey, this one's got character."

"This one has a lawsuit."

He laughed.

The fundraiser was meant to pay for safer pier railings and a storage shed so equipment wouldn't sit exposed to saltwater all winter. Greg had offered music. Mara had offered food. Tamsin had offered to oversee the repairs. Somewhere between the promises, nobody had agreed who would collect donations or clean up afterward.

I borrowed a pencil from Pip and crossed GREG off the tasks he hadn't been asked to own.

"Somebody still has to do those," he said.

"Yes. Somebody can volunteer."

"What if they don't?"

"Then we scale down the event. We don't pretend you owe free labor to everyone because you know how to play a guitar."

He sat on the edge of the stage. His expression softened, then tightened.

"Sometimes it feels like if I say no, the whole thing falls apart."

"Then the thing was badly designed."

He looked at me.

"That's a weirdly comforting insult to an event."

"One of my specialties."

We spent an hour asking people what they could actually do. Katara said her clinic volunteers could help with refreshments for an hour, not all night. Danse agreed to check the temporary stage railings but would not sign off on the damaged western section. Iroh could supervise tea and cleanup until dusk; after that, he had an appointment of his own.

Nola arrived for the sound check carrying a case of cables and a schedule that looked significantly less forgiving than Greg's hopeful volunteer sheet.

"Which of these jobs is paid?" she asked.

Greg read the paper. "Uh. None of them?"

"Then my crew's only doing the work in the contract. We have another booking tomorrow morning."

She wasn't being cruel. She was watching two sound technicians haul expensive equipment across a damp pier while half the volunteers argued about a banner.

Greg scratched his beard. "I was going to do the teardown myself."

"You can't disconnect a stage you're still playing on," Nola said.

"Well, when you put it that way."

Maui appeared carrying the marked stack of chairs. "Fear not! The great Maui can clear the entire pier with one hand."

"Please use both," Tamsin called from the railing. "And don't stack them in the exit."

Maui looked as though somebody had insulted the artistry of his shoulders. Greg grinned and tried a little drumroll on a chair seat. The chair squealed.

"Don't give him percussion," I said.

Nola checked the booking sheet. She moved the sound test earlier and made a separate line for the load-out crew. Danse could check the approved stage railings, but the electrical load would still have to be signed off by the responsible technician.

Greg listened to the new timing. "So two sets, no mystery third set, and I don't become a chair company afterward."

"Correct," Nola said.

He hummed a rising four-note phrase. It sounded like relief.

Maui stopped beside us. "Where's my name on the program?"

"Under chairs," I told him.

He sighed. "You people refuse to recognize an artist."

Maui offered to carry every chair personally.

I handed him the stack labeled FIFTEEN CHAIRS, TWO PEOPLE.

He read it.

"You're limiting my heroism."

"I'm improving its scheduling."

The sound check introduced a new problem.

Greg's amplifier buzzed when the stage crew switched on the lantern string. Danse watched the voltage meter and asked to shut the shared circuit down until they could identify the load.

“Hey, no argument here,” Greg said. “I've already had one amp go out with a pop. Not doing that on purpose.”

Maui appeared beside them with a coil of cable balanced on his hook. “I can hang the lanterns from the tallest post. Boom. Problem solved.”

“Problem relocated,” Danse corrected. “The post hasn't been inspected for that load.”

Maui looked offended. “I've lifted islands.”

“And we appreciate the resume,” Greg said. “But the island probably didn't have a building inspector.”

I laughed; Maui did not. He put the cable down and asked how he could help without making the power problem worse. Nola directed him to the approved string of unlit lanterns at the back of the square. He carried them with the grave solemnity of someone demonstrating world-shaking restraint.

Greg checked the amplifier's cable, turned the gain down, and waited while the qualified technician tested a separate circuit. The replacement power lead didn't reach as far as the original, so he agreed to a smaller stage area and changed the set list to suit the room.

“You okay with being less loud?” I asked him.

“Less loud?” he said, aghast. “Jasper, I can make an acoustic guitar sound embarrassing all by itself.”

Danse recorded the permitted load. Maui came back carrying the folding chairs he'd been assigned. They both looked pleased with work that hadn't required a dramatic announcement.

It wasn't a contest over who could save the concert. People had come to hear music and raise money for repairs. We were trying not to give them another repair bill.


At noon we had six volunteers, a safe seating plan, and a stage that did not require anyone to stand on the broken section. Greg looked at the sheet, then at me.

"You know the terrible thing?"

"What?"

"It works."

"I do hate it when that happens."

The first guests arrived while Greg tuned his guitar. Some came from Beach City; others wandered over from the Lanternwell Square market. A child asked whether all the songs would be about doors. Greg promised at least one about chairs, which earned me a look from Mara that could have curdled milk.

A man wearing a wide brown hat stopped beside the stage.

"You're Greg Universe, right?"

"That's me."

"Great! Heard you were playing all night. Can you do another three songs after the fundraiser? My kid's a huge fan."

Greg smiled out of reflex.

"Uh, maybe—"

I watched the word forming.

Then he stopped.

"Actually," he said, "I've agreed to two sets. I can sign the kid's program afterward if they want, but I've got to help with the equipment before heading home."

The man blinked.

"You're not doing an encore?"

"Not tonight."

For a terrible second, I thought the man might argue. Instead, he shrugged and went to find seats.

Greg turned toward me, looking almost surprised.

"That was uncomfortable."

"And?"

"And the sky did not fall."

"Good. We're running low on replacement sky."

He laughed, then reached for my hand. His fingers were rough against my palm from the guitar strings.

"You okay with me learning this slowly?" he asked.

"I'd be suspicious if you learned it all at once."

The concert went well enough to feel like a real concert instead of a miracle. One microphone buzzed. The first song began a little late because a child dropped a cup in the front row. The audience sang the chorus of Greg's old road song louder than he did.

Halfway through the second set, a light on the pier flickered.

Danse stood at once.

Greg stopped playing.

"Problem?"

"Power fluctuation. Keep everyone off the western platform."

There was no panic. We had actually rehearsed what to do.

Maui helped move chairs to the safer end. Katara brought the children to the square. Greg put down his guitar and checked the speaker plugs while Danse tested the line. They found a loose connection and decided not to restart the stage circuit.

The remaining songs would be acoustic.

"I can do acoustic," Greg announced to the audience. "It's mostly what I do anyway."

Someone cheered.

The night finished with a small circle of people and no dramatic lighting. I preferred it. Greg's voice carried across the water, catching in the warm space between the lanterns. I could see how tired he was, and how happy he was that he hadn't spent the whole evening trying to be four people at once.

When the final note faded, he looked at me over the strings.

I smiled.

He smiled back.

Then he stood up and helped fold the first chair.

"You're not allowed to do all of them," I reminded him.

"Just this one."

"Fine."

We stacked them in pairs, carried equipment to the dry storeroom, and counted the donation box with Mara present. The fundraiser would cover the railings, not the new shed. That was less than we'd hoped. It was enough to begin.

The last guest left with a paper cup of tea and the promise that the next event would have a proper cleanup roster.

Greg and I walked toward the Starwake Door after midnight.

He was carrying only his guitar. I was carrying the repaired volunteer sheet, folded small enough to fit in my pocket.

"Good night?" I asked.

"Best one I've had in a while."

"Even without an encore?"

"Especially without one."

He tucked a loose strand of hair behind my ear. The touch was gentle, a question rather than a claim.

"Can I give you one private encore?"

"Depends. Is it about chairs?"

"No promises."

I kissed him before he could invent a second verse.

Later, when the van door closed behind us, we left the music and the rest of the evening to ourselves.

In the morning, Greg found the volunteer sheet on the dashboard. Under my handwriting he'd added a new rule:

GREG IS ALLOWED TO BE A MUSICIAN, NOT A FURNITURE COMPANY.

I added one more line beneath it.

JASPER IS NOT THE ENTIRE MANAGEMENT DEPARTMENT EITHER.

He kissed my cheek while I wrote.

We both liked the amended version.
editorial_pass20_note: Ground Greg's affection in family, gear, volunteer costs, and polyamory without philosophical overgeneralization.
